title: Address poisoning and strange gifts
takeaway: Copy addresses only from your own saved source, never from your history, and ignore offers you did not expect.

cards.title: Your history has a twin
cards.body: You send USDC to your exchange every week. Today your history shows a new transfer from an address that starts and ends just like your exchange. Next to it is a free token with a link. Neither is a gift.

value.label: Your real exchange deposit
value.why: This is the transfer you made.

value.label: Zero value lookalike transfer
value.why: A lookalike address planted in your history.

value.label: Token with a link
value.why: The claim site is the trap.

cards.title: Address poisoning
cards.body: Scammers make an address that starts and ends like one you use. They drop it into your history with a zero value transfer or fake token. If you copy from history, you pay them. Copy from your own saved source: the exchange's deposit page each time, or your address book.
points: A zero transfer does not mean you were hacked.

cards.title: Gifts you did not ask for
cards.body: Strange NFTs or tokens can appear with a link in their name. Holding them is not the danger. The claim site is the trap: it asks for an approval that lets scammers move your assets. You can hide it in your wallet.
points: Unexpected airdrop: do not visit the link.
Do not swap or sell unknown tokens.

cards.title: Lookalike names and fake offers
cards.body: Wallet names that end in .eth can use lookalike letters, like a Cyrillic е in place of an English e. Type the name yourself and check its address matches what your friend gave you. A stranger offering a high price for your dragon by DM is a lure. Accept offers only on the marketplace you opened.

cards.body: A collector messages you about your dragon. Tap each red flag, then Done.

questions.stem: You need to send ETH to your exchange. Where do you copy the deposit address?
options: The exchange's deposit page, fresh each time
Your wallet's recent activity, the last send
The block explorer page of your last deposit
A message from exchange support with it
questions.why: Scammers plant lookalike addresses in your history. Copy from the exchange's own deposit page every time.

questions.why: The zero value transfer plants a lookalike address, and the token's claim site is a trap. Your own transfer is fine.

questions.stem: A Dragon Pass NFT you never bought appears in your wallet with claim at a site. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, skip the link, hide it
Visit the link to see what it is
Sell it fast before it is gone
Send it back to the sender
questions.why: The gift is bait. The claim site asks for an approval that lets scammers take your assets.

questions.stem: Your friend's address and one in your history share the first and last four characters. What do you do?
options: Use your saved contact, or ask your friend
Send, four characters on each end match
Copy the newest one, it must be theirs
Send a small test amount to both first
questions.why: Lookalike addresses copy the start and end. Use your saved contact or ask your friend directly.

seg.label: Too good, too urgent
seg.why: Unexpected offers with deadlines are bait.

seg.label: Unknown trade site
seg.why: Use only the marketplace you open yourself.

questions.why: An unexpected offer with a deadline and its own site is a lure. Check offers only on the marketplace you opened yourself.

questions.stem: A friend's wallet name ending in .eth arrives in a DM. It looks right. What do you do?
options: Check its address matches the one your friend gave you
Paste it, the letters look exactly the same
Send it, ENS names are unique and cannot be copied
Trust it if your friend's avatar shows next to it
questions.why: Lookalike letters can make two names look the same. Type the name yourself and check the address matches the one your friend gave you.

questions.stem: You received 5,000 free tokens. A site says you can swap them for ETH. What do you do?
options: Leave them alone, do not swap or sell
Swap them on that site before the price drops
Approve them first, then swap on that site
Send a few to a friend to test them
questions.why: Do not swap or sell unknown tokens. The swap site can ask for an approval that drains you.

questions.why: A surprise gift, an unknown site and a deadline. Trust only links checked on two official channels.

questions.stem: Your history shows a 0 USDC transfer from your address that you did not make. What does it mean?
options: Someone planted a lookalike address in your history
Your seed phrase leaked, so move everything now
Your exchange sent a test transfer to check you
A refund arrived, but the amount shows wrong
questions.why: Zero value transfers need no approval from you. They plant a lookalike address so you copy it later.

questions.stem: A buyer DMs you a high offer and a link to accept it. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, check offers on your own marketplace
Accept it fast, high offers do not last
Open the link, but only to read it
Reply asking for proof of funds first
questions.why: Offers you did not expect are lures. Fake offer links can ask for a listing signature that sells your dragon.
